Changelog

Source: NEWS.md

multiScaleAC 0.2.0

First release of the multiScaleAC() interface. The package is renamed from KernelCommunication to multiScaleAC, matching the companion manuscript; the repository keeps its old name, because that is the URL the paper prints.

Earlier releases contained only soupir_moran_multi() and soupir_moran_bv(). Both are unchanged, remain exported, and are not deprecated — soupir_moran_multi() is the reference implementation the whole test suite is pinned to. So results computed with previous versions are unaffected by this release.

New: the multiScaleAC interface

  • multiScaleAC() computes the bivariate Moran’s I curve over a bandwidth vector and returns an S4 kernelcomm_result. Working memory is O(N × length(h)), with no N × N matrix at any point: 256 MB at N = 7122 against 2225 MB for the reference, and N = 20000 runs in 440 MB. Results match the reference exactly.
  • multiScaleAC_batch() runs many samples, optionally forked across cores, with per-sample checkpoint files so an interrupted batch resumes where it stopped.
  • compute_significance() and adjust_pvalues() for inference, kept separate from computation so one curve can be tested several ways.
  • suggest_bandwidths() and qc_neighborhoods() for choosing and checking bandwidths, and validate_inputs() for pre-flight checks.
  • plot(), summary(), print(), show(), plus plot_scale_curve(), plot_permutation_distribution(), plot_batch_comparison() and plot_significance_summary().
  • export_mxfda() and export_mxfda_batch() for handing curves to functional data analysis, as the manuscript does with FPCA.

Inference

  • Permutation p-values, permuting only the second gene. alternative defaults to "greater", the manuscript’s one-tailed upper test; "less" and "two.sided" are available. estimator offers (r+1)/(n+1) (default, cannot return zero) or the manuscript’s r/n.

  • The whole-curve supremum test the manuscript defines, in sup_p_value. It needs no multiplicity correction across bandwidths, which matters because bandwidths of one gene pair are strongly dependent.

  • Exact analytical moments of the permutation null. The statistic is a linear permutation statistic, so the first four moments of its null and the full cross-bandwidth covariance have closed forms. They cost O(N) per bandwidth and are computed by default. compute_significance(method = "moment") uses them; method = "auto" uses them only where diagnostics say a continuous approximation is trustworthy; multiScaleAC(permute = "flagged") draws permutations only where they are needed.

    The gain is resolution rather than speed. With 999 permutations the smallest reportable p-value is 1/1000, so p = 0.001 and p = 1e-6 are indistinguishable, and resolving 1e-5 needs about 100,000 permutations. The moments have no such floor and agree with a 499,999-permutation run to under 1%.

    The moments are exact; mapping them to a tail probability is not. The default mapping was chosen by measurement against 200,000 permutations rather than by theory, and inst/validation/results/README.md records the comparison, including two outcomes that contradict what theory would predict.

  • null_lower and null_upper give the null envelope: quantiles of the permutation distribution, showing where the statistic falls under complete spatial randomness. They are not a confidence interval for the observed value, and the envelope level is set separately from the test threshold.

  • z_scores is an effect size only. Do not convert it with pnorm(): the permutation null is skewed whenever the expression data is, and on the bundled example data a normal approximation is anti-conservative by two orders of magnitude in the tail.

Bandwidth units

Bandwidths are in the units of coords, and this is the easiest way to get a meaningless result. ccRCCExample is in millimetres, spanning 1.02 mm with a median nearest-neighbour distance of 0.0073 mm, so useful bandwidths are about 0.01 to 0.25 — which is the manuscript’s 10–250 micrometres expressed in this dataset’s units. Passing h = 25 drives every pairwise weight above 0.9999, making the kernel effectively constant and collapsing I(h) toward zero for every gene pair.

qc_neighborhoods() reports a saturation column for exactly this, and a test fails if any fixture uses a bandwidth in that regime.

Kernels and distances

"gaussian" (default, and what the manuscript uses), "uniform" and "exponential" kernels; "euclidean", "manhattan" and "minkowski" distances. All run inside the same tiled core, so none can bypass the eps predicate or the zero-row-sum policy. User-supplied kernel and distance functions are still supported and take an R fallback path.

eps defaults to 0, meaning no thresholding, which is the point of the method: computing the statistic without discarding low weights is what distinguishes it from approaches that filter low kernel density estimates first. Raising it is supported but changes the estimand.

nan_policy makes the zero-row-sum behaviour explicit. The default reproduces the reference implementation, which reports 0 for an entire affected bandwidth.

Also in this release

  • lag.sparse() is renamed lag_sparse(). The old name was only ever registered as an S3 method for a class that Matrix objects do not have, so it was never callable and no shim is provided.
  • Compiled objects and shared libraries are no longer tracked in git, and the source tarball no longer ships development notes, the manuscript PDF or build artefacts.
  • man/rcpp_hello_world.Rd, which documented a function that does not exist, is removed.
  • README, this file, and vignette("multiScaleAC").

Testing

451 tests, pinned to soupir_moran_multi(), which is never modified and is hash-guarded by a test so it cannot drift. Fixtures are generated from it alone, at unit-correct bandwidths, and cover the degenerate cases — isolated cells, zero-variance genes, saturated and empty kernels — as well as the ordinary ones. R CMD check --as-cran runs the examples, the tests and the vignette.
